# Pitch–intensity coordination in wild chimpanzee (Pan troglodytes)

# vocalizations: a robust within-call pattern, not an ontogenetic one

Jenny M. Michlich, AM1,2,3

1Department of Animal Behavior and Welfare, Husson University, Bangor, ME, USA

2School of Complex Adaptive Systems, Arizona State University, Tempe, AZ, USA 3Department of Biology, Community College of Allegheny County, Pittsburgh, PA, USA

Corresponding author: Jenny M. Michlich, michlichj@husson.edu

## Abstract

Pitch–intensity covariation, or the tendency for fundamental frequency (F0) and vocal intensity to move in the same direction within a vocalization, has been proposed as a marker of maturing vocal-motor control, as the two parameters are driven by separate physiological systems that presumably must be actively coordinated rather than simply co-occurring. I tested this idea in wild chimpanzees using archival Gombe field recordings spanning infancy to adolescence (15 individuals). Voiced segments (n = 8,874) were classified with a ToBI-inspired pitch-accent × boundary-tone scheme, and two coordination metrics were computed: directional covariation across a segment's thirds, and the timing offset between peak F0 and peak intensity. Every subject in this sample showed higher covariation in the later portion of a call than the earlier portion (Wilcoxon W = 0, p < 0.001), and this held with no difference in magnitude across age classes (p = 0.73), which I take to reflect a developmentally invariant, likely physiologically grounded pattern rather than anything specific to maturation. Age-class differences in overall covariation did not reach significance under a conservative permutation test, though the adolescent-versus-infant contrast reflected a large effect size (d = 1.76) that this study was simply underpowered (66%) to confirm, which is a different conclusion than the infant-versus-juvenile contrast (d = 0.02), which looks like a true null. The peak-timing offset metric complicated this picture further by identifying a different age class as its outlier, which I take as a caution against overinterpreting either result on its own. Taken together, chimpanzee vocalizations appear to show a robust, age-invariant within-call coordination pattern, while the evidence for an ontogenetic trend remains inconclusive and would benefit from larger samples going forward.

Keywords: chimpanzee; vocal development; pitch–intensity coordination; ToBI; bioacoustics; ontogeny

## Introduction

It is worth starting with what pitch–intensity coordination actually requires physiologically, since it is easy to assume the two simply move together. F0 is controlled primarily by laryngeal musculature, namely vocal fold tension and length, while intensity is driven largely by subglottal pressure generated by the respiratory system (Titze 1994); the airflow driving phonation itself varies across taxa and even within a single species' own repertoire, with pulmonic egressive airflow the most common mechanism but by no means the only one (Eklund 2008). Because F0 and intensity are produced by anatomically and neurally distinct systems, any consistent covariation between them within a call is not something we should expect for free; it requires active coordination rather than passive physical coupling. In human infants, the shift from largely reflexive phonation to voluntary, motor-controlled vocalization over the first months of life is accompanied by increasing coordination between respiratory and laryngeal control (Lester and Boukydis 1985; Green et al. 2000), which is what originally motivated the idea, explored here, that pitch–intensity coordination could serve as an acoustic proxy for the maturation of vocal-motor control more broadly, including in species other than our own.

Wild chimpanzee (Pan troglodytes) vocalizations have been the focus of increasing acoustic and developmental interest in recent years (Grawunder et al. 2022; Bortolato et al. 2022), and this work builds on a much longer tradition of describing primate vocal repertoires and their ontogeny more generally (Marler 1976; Goodall 1986; Lameira, Maddieson, and Zuberbühler 2014). It is worth noting up front that ontogenetic change in chimpanzee vocalization is not purely a matter of motor control: the supralaryngeal vocal tract itself changes shape substantially over the course of development, independent of any change in neural or muscular coordination (Nishimura 2005). This means that age-related acoustic differences reported here, or in any comparable study, have to be interpreted with the possibility of concurrent anatomical change in mind, and I return to this point in the Limitations. Whether chimpanzee vocal development additionally shows a shift toward tighter motor coordination, potentially detectable in the timing and directional relationship between pitch and intensity contours, has not, to my knowledge, been directly tested using a segment-level acoustic classification approach, which is the gap this paper tries to fill.

A separate, but related, question that is worth raising here is whether frameworks built to describe the phonological structure of human language can be meaningfully applied to non-human vocal systems at all. This is a question that has been asked, in one form or another, across a fairly wide range of taxa: structured, referential alarm calls in vervet monkeys (Seyfarth, Cheney, and Marler 1980), phonological and combinatorial organization in bird song (Suzuki 2016; Engesser, Fitch, and Huybregts 2021), compositional structure spanning animal and human systems (Townsend et al. 2018), phonetic analysis of humpback whale song units (Pines 2018), and more explicit critical treatments of whether the theoretical toolkit of phonology transfers usefully to non-human systems in the first place (Yip 2006). I do not take a strong position on this debate here. Instead, following what seems to be this literature's general strategy

To get at this, I adapted a classification scheme derived from the autosegmental-metrical (AM) framework of intonational phonology, in which vocalizations are labeled using Tones and Break Indices (ToBI)-style pitch-accent and boundary-tone categories (Beckman and Hirschberg 1994; Jun 2005; see Hayes et al. 2013 for general background on the phonological theory this framework is built on). ToBI was, of course, developed to describe human intonational phonology, but its underlying acoustic primitives, namely the direction and shape of local pitch excursions and the pitch level found at phrase edges, do not presuppose any human-specific linguistic structure. This makes it a reasonably theory-light starting point for describing non-human vocal contours, though how well it actually transfers is a question I come back to in the Discussion. It is worth noting that ToBI is not the only automatic system built around this general idea of stylizing an F0 curve and then symbolically coding its target points; the Momel/INTSINT system (Hirst and Espesser 1993; Hirst, Di Cristo, and Espesser 2000) takes a related approach, fitting a quadratic spline to the macro-prosodic component of the pitch curve and then coding the resulting target points with a small, language-independent tonal alphabet. I did not adopt Momel/INTSINT here, since the ToBI-style pitch-accent and boundary-tone categories map more directly onto the initial/medial/final segment structure used throughout this analysis, but the general strategy of separating a stylized pitch curve from a symbolic coding of it is one this study shares with that tradition.

Here I report two acoustic metrics of pitch–intensity coordination, directional covariation and peak-timing offset, computed from segment-level classifications of archival Gombe chimpanzee recordings spanning infancy to adolescence. I use these to test two things: first, whether either metric shows a consistent structural pattern that holds regardless of age, and second, whether either metric shows evidence of an ontogenetic trend consistent with maturing vocal-motor control.

## Methods

Subjects and recordings

The vocalizations analyzed here were drawn from the Gombe chimpanzee archive deposited on Dryad (DOI 10.5061/dryad.5tq80), which consists of analog field recordings made in the early 1970s and later digitized at 96 kHz/24-bit by the Macaulay Library (see Plooij et al. 2015 for a fuller description of this longitudinal recording archive). I selected fifteen focal individuals to span infancy through adolescence (Table 1), based on ages recorded in the archive's accompanying metadata, namely the age given at each catalogued recording date, with the reported range spanning each individual's earliest to latest catalogued recording. Pitch and intensity were extracted using Praat (Boersma and Weenink 2023) via the parselmouth Python interface (Jadoul, Thompson, and de Boer 2018). Fundamental frequency was extracted with the cross-correlation method (100–2000 Hz range), and intensity with a minimum periodicity of 200 Hz, following settings reported for chimpanzee vocalizations by Grawunder et al. (2022).

Segmentation

Each continuous recording's pitch track was partitioned into discrete voiced segments by identifying gaps exceeding 20 ms during which no pitch value was detected. Candidate segments shorter than 30 ms were discarded. Given recording durations of approximately 6–64 minutes per subject, this yielded 129–2,259 voiced segments per individual (median 508; total 10,247 across all subjects before quality filtering; see Quality control below). Very long recordings (>40 minutes) were processed in sequential sub-segments to manage memory constraints, with segment timestamps corrected back onto each individual's continuous timeline prior to analysis.

Prosodic contour classification

Each segment was assigned a pitch-accent and boundary-tone label from a six-category × four-category ToBI-inspired scheme (pitch accents: H*, L*, L*+H, L+H*, H+!H*, H*!H*; boundary tones: L-L%, L-H%, H-L%, H-H%). Classification was performed algorithmically from the shape of each segment's pitch contour: the segment was divided into initial, medial, and final thirds; onset level relative to the segment median, the slope across the first two-thirds of the segment, and the number of local maxima in a smoothed contour (prominence-based peak detection) determined the pitch-accent category; the pitch level of the medial third and the slope and endpoint level of the final portion determined the boundary-tone category.

Pitch–intensity coordination metrics

For each segment, pitch and intensity values were each averaged within the initial, medial, and final thirds. A segment was classified as covarying across a given half (initial-to-medial or medial-to-final) if the direction of change in mean pitch across that half matched the direction of change in mean intensity across the same half. Separately, the peak-timing offset was computed as the signed time difference between each segment's point of maximum pitch and point of maximum intensity (intensity linearly interpolated onto the pitch time grid).

Segment-final pitch level and subsequent pause duration

As a further, structurally distinct test of whether pitch level at a segment's edge relates to the strength of the following juncture, we examined the relationship between a segment's boundary-tone classification and the duration of silence preceding the next detected segment within the same continuous recording. For each pair of temporally adjacent segments, the segment-final pitch level (the second element of its boundary-tone label, H or L) and the duration

Quality control

Frame-to-frame pitch ratios outside the range [0.6, 1.7] were flagged as possible octave-tracking errors, in which the cross-correlation pitch tracker may have locked onto half or double the true fundamental frequency for part of a segment. Manual inspection of flagged segments against corresponding spectrograms confirmed that this heuristic reliably identified segments containing an implausible intra-segment frequency jump (e.g., F0 measured near 110 Hz for part of a segment before jumping to approximately 1200 Hz within under 200 ms) while not flagging segments with unusually low but internally consistent pitch throughout. Flagged segments (13.4% of the 10,247 originally detected; 12.3% of infant, 11.0% of juvenile, and 18.9% of adolescent segments) were excluded from all reported analyses, leaving 8,874 segments.

As a further, independent check on pitch-tracking accuracy among the retained (non-flagged) segments, a stratified random sample of 24 segments was drawn (8 per age class, spanning 8 subjects), and 20 of these (limited by file availability) were inspected visually by overlaying the extracted F0 contour on the corresponding spectrogram. Each segment was classified as accurate (the extracted contour followed a visible harmonic band directly, or was related to a more prominent visible band by a clear integer multiple, e.g., a tracked fundamental with a clean second harmonic at twice its frequency), ambiguous (spectrographic energy was too faint to independently confirm or disconfirm the tracked contour), or problematic (the segment's acoustic energy was broadband and non-harmonic, e.g., percussive, such that pitch tracking is not well defined). Sixteen of 20 segments (80%) were classified as accurate, three (15%) as ambiguous due to low signal-to-noise ratio, and one (5%) as problematic, involving a broadband acoustic event inconsistent with tonal vocalization (Figure 2).

Statistical treatment

Given that segments within a call, and calls within a subject, are not independent observations, and that per-class subject counts are small (4–6 subjects), two complementary approaches were used. First, the within-call asymmetry (covariation in the medial-to-final versus initial-to-medial half) was tested using a paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test across subjects (one mean value per subject per half), the most directly comparable non-parametric paired test for this design. Second, age-class comparisons of overall covariation and peak-timing offset used each subject's mean value as a single, independent data point (n = 6, 5, 4), with group differences assessed via a permutation test (20,000 resamples of subject-to-class labels, respecting observed group sizes) rather than parametric tests, since this approach makes no distributional assumptions and directly respects the true number of independent sampling units. Effect sizes (Cohen's d) and post hoc statistical power, given the observed effect size and actual subject counts, were computed for each pairwise age-class comparison to distinguish negligible effects from effects that were simply underpowered to detect at conventional significance thresholds.

The permutation test above treats all 15 subjects as exchangeable, independent sampling units. This assumption is not entirely correct: archival biographical records accompanying the same Dryad deposit (Gombe_biography-for_1971-3; Plooij et al. 2015) show that two pairs of subjects are, in fact, maternal siblings — Gremlin and Goblin, both offspring of the female Melissa, and Prof and Pom, both offspring of the female Passion — and in both pairs, one sibling falls in the infant class and the other in the juvenile class. Shared maternal identity is a plausible source of non-independence between subjects (e.g., a mother's own vocal style, rearing behavior, or rank could influence her offsprings' vocal development independent of age), which the subject-level

A universal within-call asymmetry, independent of age

Every one of the 15 subjects showed higher pitch–intensity covariation in the medial-to-final third of a call than in the initial-to-medial third (paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test, W = 0, p < 0.001; mean within-subject difference 8.9 percentage points), which I take to be the most robust finding in this dataset. What is perhaps more telling is that the size of this within-call asymmetry did not differ significantly across age classes (Kruskal-Wallis H = 0.62, p = 0.73; mean gap: infant 8.0, juvenile 8.7, adolescent 10.5 percentage points), suggesting this is not something that changes as the animal matures.

Peak-timing offset

The time offset between each segment's peak pitch and peak intensity tells a somewhat different story than covariation does. Mean absolute offset was 34.6 ms for infants, 40.4 ms for juveniles, and 34.3 ms for adolescents, with the juvenile class, rather than adolescence, standing out as the outlier group here. Effect sizes were: juvenile vs. infant, d = 0.89; juvenile vs. adolescent, d = 0.60; infant vs. adolescent, d = 0.04, which is a near-zero effect and notably different from what the covariation comparison showed for this same pair of classes. None of these age-class comparisons reached significance under the same permutation test (all p > 0.24). Looking at the individual subjects, it became clear that the juvenile elevation was being driven substantially by just one subject (mean offset 57.0 ms, compared with 35–36 ms for the other four juveniles), which is worth keeping in mind before reading too much into this class-level pattern.

Segment-final pitch level and subsequent pause duration

Segments ending on a high pitch level were, as it turns out, followed by longer silences than segments ending on a low pitch level, and this held at the level of individual subjects: 11 of the 15 subjects showed this direction, and the difference reached significance under a paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test across subjects (W = 11, p = 0.0034; mean within-subject difference 274 ms). As I noted in the Methods, this is asking a structurally different question than whether a boundary occurs at all, since every segment edge in this dataset is already a boundary by construction. What this result actually shows, then, is that among boundaries that already exist, the pitch level right at that boundary predicts how long the following pause tends to be, and it should not be read as a test of boundary presence itself.

## Discussion

What I take to be the central, statistically robust finding of this study is, somewhat ironically, not a developmental one at all. Every subject, regardless of age, showed tighter pitch–intensity coordination in the latter portion of a vocalization than in the earlier portion, and the size of this effect was indistinguishable across infant, juvenile, and adolescent age classes. I think this pattern is best explained by a general physiological account of vocalization on a single respiratory cycle, which I lay out below.

Physiological basis: the breath-group hypothesis

Lieberman (1967) proposed the breath group as a physiologically grounded unit of intonational structure, defined as the portion of an utterance produced on a single expiration, and I think this is the right place to look for an explanation of what I am seeing here. In Lieberman's account, the “unmarked” breath group, the one associated with declarative, finality-signaling intonation, is characterized by relatively steady laryngeal (cricothyroid) tension throughout phonation while subglottal air pressure declines as the lungs empty, producing a characteristic fall in F0 toward the end of the expiration unless the speaker actively counteracts it. The “marked” breath group, associated instead with non-finality and question intonation, involves an increase in laryngeal

tension toward the end of phonation that counteracts the falling subglottal pressure, producing a non-falling or rising terminal F0 (Lieberman 1967; Lieberman, Sawashima, Harris, and Gay 1970). This relationship was later quantified directly: Lieberman, Knudson, and Mead (1969) measured the rate of change of F0 with respect to subglottal pressure during sustained phonation, which gives us an empirical sense of how much a given decline in respiratory drive should lower F0 when there is no active laryngeal compensation happening. Collier (1975) extended this account to intensity, arguing that the same declining subglottal pressure that drives F0 declination is also what drives the parallel decline in intensity that is commonly observed across an utterance. In other words, F0 and intensity may well share a common physiological driver, one whose default, uncorrected trajectory over a single expiration is downward in both parameters together.

I should say that this account has not gone unchallenged, and it would not be honest to present it as settled. Some authors have questioned whether subglottal pressure changes are themselves sufficient to explain the full pattern of observed F0 change, and there has been ongoing debate over how much of declination is passive respiratory decay versus active, linguistically-controlled behavior (see the exchange between Lieberman 1986 and ’t Hart, and Vaissière 1983 for a broader review of the physiological explanations on offer). I am not taking a position here on the strong form of the passive-declination hypothesis. What I do think is defensible is the narrower claim that a shared respiratory driver of F0 and intensity remains a plausible and physiologically motivated contributor to their coordination within a call, regardless of exactly how the passive and actively-controlled components end up balancing out.

Vaissière (2005) points out that this same archetypal rise-then-fall pattern of F0 and intensity over a single expiration “is a pattern shared by non-human primates and infant cry”, citing Lieberman (1967), which suggests a physiological mechanism common across vocalizing mammals rather than something specific to adult human speech. If pitch and intensity in chimpanzee vocalizations are likewise both partly governed by a shared, declining respiratory drive over the course of a call, then a tightening of their directional coupling as air runs low toward the end of the call, which is exactly the pattern I observed here in all 15 subjects, is a natural physiological consequence that has little to do with age or species. It does not, in other words, need a separate motor-learning story to explain it. This physiological grounding is also not limited to the production side: even early, subcortical stages of auditory processing show measurable sensitivity to the pitch and intensity structure of vocalizations, for instance brainstem responses to speech that track acoustic features associated with emotional prosody (Wang, Nicol, Skoe, Sams, and Kraus 2010). This is consistent with pitch–intensity structure being a fairly basic, biologically fundamental feature of vocal communication on both the production and perception sides, rather than something built specifically for language or higher cognition.

The evidence for an age-related trend in overall pitch–intensity covariation, by contrast, is inconclusive rather than negative, and I want to be careful about that distinction. A conservative, subject-level permutation test, which I think is the most defensible approach given that there are only 15 independent sampling units in this dataset, found no age-class comparison reaching significance. That said, I do not think this null result should be read the same way across the board. The infant-versus-juvenile comparison showed an effect size near zero, and this is plausibly a genuine absence of difference. The adolescent-versus-infant comparison is a different matter: it showed a large effect size that the present sample was simply underpowered to confirm, and what is needed to settle this is a considerably larger sample of subjects, not a different analytical approach.

A further reason for caution, and one I think is worth taking seriously, is that the two acoustic metrics of pitch–intensity coordination used here, directional covariation and peak-timing offset, identified different age classes as the apparent outlier group: adolescence for covariation, the juvenile class for offset. The juvenile-class effect was itself, as noted above, being driven substantially by a single subject. This kind of divergence between related but non-identical acoustic measures of prosodic coordination is not without precedent in the human literature. Erickson (2010), for instance, found that articulatory jaw-opening rhythm and ToBI-transcribed intonational phrasing, while both plausible indices of prosodic organization in the same utterances, diverge once contrastive emphasis is introduced, which is a case of two legitimate measures of prosodic structure disagreeing about where the important variation actually lies. I take the disagreement between my own two metrics here as a reason for caution rather than as evidence favoring one metric's story over the other.

It is worth remembering that the ToBI-inspired classification scheme used here was adapted from a framework built for human intonational phonology, and designed, in its fullest form, to capture cross-linguistic variation in how prominence and phrasing get marked (Jun 2005). Jun's typological synthesis makes the point that not every human language actually uses the full pitch-accent inventory; some languages mark prominence and phrasing mostly through edge, or boundary, tones instead of pitch accents. My finding that chimpanzee vocalizations lean overwhelmingly on simple, non-bitonal pitch accents and a small handful of boundary-tone combinations, with the more elaborate compound categories doing very little of the classificatory work, fits with chimpanzee vocal prosody occupying a fairly simple corner of the typological space this framework was built to describe, rather than needing its full inventory. There is also a practical takeaway here: statistics computed within any of the rare compound-accent categories, each under 135 segments pooled across all 15 subjects, rest on a much thinner evidential base than statistics computed on the two dominant simple accents, and I would interpret those cautiously.

The finding that segment-final pitch level predicts how long the following pause tends to be has a structural analog, though not a direct parallel, in the human speech-processing literature. Wang and Hirschberg (1992) found that whether the word preceding a potential intonational phrase

## Limitations

The principal limitation concerns sample size. The effective unit for age-class comparisons is the number of subjects (4–6 per class), not the number of segments, and the classes are further unbalanced and, in two cases, drawn from families that overlap across classes (see Table 3). As the sensitivity analysis above demonstrates, this renders the infant-versus-juvenile null result less settled than it initially appears, and it should be treated as unresolved rather than confirmed.

Two additional points warrant mention: call type was not controlled for and could plausibly differ by age class (a corpus method such as collostructional analysis, Gries 2014, could help address this in future work); and separately, the chimpanzee vocal tract itself continues to develop anatomically alongside any change in motor control (Nishimura 2005), such that this study cannot fully disentangle the two.

## Conclusion

Chimpanzee vocalizations, at least in this sample, show a robust, age-invariant asymmetry in pitch–intensity coordination between the earlier and later portions of a call, and I think this is best explained by general primate vocal-respiratory physiology rather than by anything developmental. Evidence for an ontogenetic trend in overall pitch–intensity coordination, on the other hand, remains genuinely inconclusive: it is not supported by the most conservative statistical test available to me, but the effect-size and power analysis suggests this is more likely a matter of insufficient sample size for at least one comparison than a confirmed absence of an effect. I would recommend that future work pursue larger and more balanced samples across age classes, ideally with call type recorded and controlled for, before anyone draws firm conclusions about the ontogeny of vocal-motor coordination in this species.

# Sequence-level recursion in nonhuman vocal communication

# A comparative test of five recursion types across 43 species

## Abstract

A recurring question in comparative bioacoustics is whether nonhuman vocal sequences show recursive structure of the kind central to human language (Yip 2006). We tested five recursion types drawn from the phonological literature on recursive prosodic structure — center-embedding, tail-end embedding, left-boundary embedding, external (prefix) phrase expansion, and internal phrase expansion — against call-type sequences from 43 species of bats, birds, primates, a pinniped, and two cetaceans. Center-embedding, tail-end embedding, and left-boundary embedding were tested across 223 files; external and internal phrase expansion were tested across a subset of 82 files spanning nine species. Center-embedding was rare overall (5.8% of files); under Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate correction, two species retained significant positive results — yellow-naped amazon (Amazona auropalliata) duets and house wren (Troglodytes aedon) song — while bowhead and humpback whale showed raw-significant but FDR-non-surviving results, indicating weaker statistical support than an uncorrected reading would suggest. Gibbon song (three species, two genera, 30 sessions) showed no center-embedding, but Hylobates agilis showed significant external and internal phrase expansion in the majority of sessions, consistent with the progressive build-up structure documented for gibbon great calls. Bowhead and humpback whale, similar in their center-embedding results, diverged sharply on phrase expansion: humpback showed pervasive repetition across all sequence positions, bowhead did not. Tail-end embedding was the most broadly replicated pattern (49.8% of files, with 97 of 112 raw-significant results surviving FDR correction); a phylogeneticallycorrected analysis found its association with vocal-learning category weakened but not eliminated relative to a naive estimate (PGLS slope = 1.01, p = 0.121, versus naive slope = 2.10, p = 0.004). The same phylogenetic treatment applied to external and internal phrase expansion was inconclusive, limited by the small number of species (n = 6) with a defined vocal-learning category. These findings are discussed in relation to the phonological recursion literature, in which recursive prosodic structure is documented as a real but non-default, minority-realized phenomenon even in human production.

Keywords: recursion; vocal learning; bioacoustics; phonology; sequence analysis; comparative cognition

## Introduction

Recursion — the embedding of a structure within a structure of the same type — has occupied a central and contested place in discussions of what, if anything, is unique about human language (Hauser, Chomsky, and Fitch 2002). The question of whether phonological structure of this kind exists outside human language was posed

directly by Yip (2006), whose call for a systematic search for phonology in other species motivates the comparative program pursued here. Center-embedded structure of the form A[B[C]B]A, in which an outer element brackets an inner one of the same category, is the paradigm case: it is well attested in human syntax and phonology, but claims of its presence in nonhuman communication remain sparse and contested. Rey, Perruchet, and Fagot (2012) demonstrated that Guinea baboons (Papio papio) could be trained to detect a center-embedded (AnBn) grammar in an operant task, raising the question of whether such structure emerges spontaneously in natural vocal sequences without training. A three-tier framework for vocal learning, distinguishing nonlearners, usage learners, and production learners (Vernes et al. 2021), provides an axis along which to ask whether sequence-level structural complexity scales with vocal-learning capacity. Recent work on self-embedded vocal motifs in wild orangutans (Lameira et al. 2023) and primate call rhythm (De Gregorio et al. 2025) has extended this comparative program to isochrony and rhythmic structure. Categorical treatment of call types, as adopted throughout this study, is independently supported in the songbird literature, where perception of call variants is categorical and context-dependent rather than continuous (Lachlan and Nowicki 2015).

The  broader  field  of  animal  linguistics  has  recently  been  surveyed  by  Suzuki  (2024),  who  identifies combinatorial and syntax-like structure in animal signals as an active area of interdisciplinary research. A landmark case is the chestnut-crowned babbler (Pomatostomus ruficeps), in which two acoustically distinct call elements are combined into different orderings associated with different behavioral contexts (Engesser et al. 2019). Bowling and Fitch (2015) caution against characterizing findings of this kind using linguistic terms such as phoneme, phonology, or syntax without qualification, since these terms are conventionally defined with reference to meaning, and meaning in animal communication is accessible only indirectly through behavioral inference. We follow this caution throughout: the analyses reported here concern statistically and acoustically defined call-type sequences, and terms such as recursion and phonological are used by structural analogy with the human linguistic literature that motivates the typology tested, not as a claim that the underlying units carry meaning in the linguistic sense. The quantitative, computational approach to analyzing animal vocal structure adopted here follows a tradition established by Clark, Marler, and Beeman (1987), who introduced computerbased methods for comparing and averaging animal vocalizations to quantify song structure and development in swamp sparrows (Melospiza georgiana).

This study addresses recursive structure within a single bout or continuous recording — the sequence of call-type units produced within one vocal sequence — referred to here as sequence-level or phonological-level recursion, by analogy with recursive structure among words or prosodic units within a single utterance in human language. Recursion at the level of the bout itself — whether whole bouts nest within larger bouts — is a distinct, structurally higher-order question not addressed here.

Five recursion types drawn from the phonological typology motivating this study were operationalized, illustrated in Figure 1. Center-embedding, tail-end embedding, and left-boundary embedding were tested at full scale. External and internal phrase expansion — concepts originating in Rothstein's (1989) and Koch's (1983) analysis of musical phrase structure and incorporated into the phonological recursion literature by Schreuder and Gilbers (2004; see also Schreuder n.d.) — were tested at a smaller scale on the subset of species most central to the findings reported here. Center-embedding is a symmetric bracketing pattern in which a sequence returns to its opening element after one or more internal elements (A…B…A). Tail-end embedding is a fixed unit repeated and iteratively appended to the end of a sequence (A[BC][BC][BC]…), the phonological analogue of what Schreuder terms  tail-recursion,  illustrated  musically  by  repeated  cadential  motion. Statistical tests

For each file, the ordered sequence of call-type labels was tested against five statistics, each compared to a null distribution of 2000 random permutations of the same symbol sequence. Center-embedding was the count of immediate ABA triplets. Tail-end embedding was the count of immediately-repeated bigrams anywhere in the sequence. Left-boundary embedding was the trend in gap size between successive occurrences of the sequence's most frequent symbol. External and internal phrase expansion were each the count of immediately-repeated bigrams restricted to the first or middle third of the sequence respectively, compared to the same statistic on permuted  sequences.  All  statistics  were  validated  on  synthetic  random-order  sequences  to  confirm  an appropriately null result, and the two expansion statistics were additionally validated on synthetic sequences engineered with genuine front-loaded or middle-loaded repetition to confirm adequate statistical power. Given the large number of tests conducted, Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) correction was applied separately within each of the three full-scale test types (center-embedding, tail-end embedding, boundary embedding) across all 223 files, at a corrected alpha of 0.05.

Phylogenetic comparative analysis

Species-level mean tail-end embedding z-scores were regressed on ordinal vocal-learning category (nonlearner = 0, usage learner = 1, production learner = 2) using ordinary least squares and phylogenetic generalized least squares (PGLS), the latter using a composite phylogeny built from published consensus divergence times spanning all sampled clades, to assess whether an apparent relationship between vocal-learning category and tailend embedding reflects independent evolution rather than shared ancestry.

## Discussion

Schreuder, Gilbers, and Quéné's work on Dutch, the source of the boundary-embedding example in Figure 1 (the compound [onafhankelijk [Amsterdams [aardrijkskundig genoötschap]]]), reports that a recursive pitch-accent marker was realized on the embedded adjective in 22% of syntactically recursive phrases in production, against a 30% baseline rate of early accent even in non-recursive control phrases. The 22% figure is the appropriate benchmark for recursion-specific realization in that study. Our replicated species show center-embedding in a comparable minority range (parrot duets, 50%; house wren, 17%; bowhead whale, 14%; humpback whale, 29%). Elfner (2015) provides an independent empirical demonstration of recursive prosodic phrasing in production, in Connemara Irish. Together these sources indicate that phonological recursion, where directly measured in human production, is a real but minority, non-categorical phenomenon.

A related theoretical debate concerns the mechanism by which recursive prosodic phrasing arises. Constraintbased analyses distinguish ALIGN-type mappings, which align a single edge of a syntactic constituent with a prosodic phrase and rarely generate recursive structure in practice, from MATCH-type mappings, which align both edges symmetrically and do generate it (Féry 2023, following Selkirk 2011). Whether recursive phrasing is the analytically preferred default or a marked exception remains unresolved in this literature, paralleling the NoRecursion debate discussed below.

Cheng and Downing (2021) argue for a restrictive use of phonological recursion, showing that apparent recursive prosodic structure in several case-study languages is not syntactically motivated and can be reanalyzed without invoking recursion. They describe a formal NoRecursion constraint (Itô and Mester 2012; Selkirk 1995; Vigário 2010; Vogel 2009, 2012, 2019) under which recursive prosodic structure is a marked exception requiring independent motivation rather than a default assumption. The present finding that center-embedding is rare overall (5.8% of files) and concentrated in four of forty-three species, each independently linked to unusually rule-governed vocal behavior, is consistent with this view of recursion as an exceptional, independently-

Absence of center-embedding does not indicate absence of recursive structure generally: Hylobates agilis shows no center-embedding but substantial external and internal phrase expansion, and the two baleen whale species tested show divergent expansion profiles despite similar center-embedding results. The five-type typology adopted here treats these as formally distinct constructs that need not co-occur, and the gibbon and whale results are consistent with that distinction.

The association between the four raw-replicated center-embedding species and independently-documented claims of syntactic or hierarchical organization was not designed in advance: no species was selected for testing on this basis, and all species were subject to an identical, pre-specified statistical procedure. This association is strongest for the two species whose results survive multiple-comparison correction, parrot duets and house wren; the whale results, while independently corroborated by descriptive literature on baleen whale song structure, currently rest on weaker statistical footing and warrant additional within-species replication before being treated as confirmed. The dissociation between the center-embedding pattern and general sequential complexity, illustrated by Bengalese finch, indicates that center-embedded recursion is separable from the finite-state syntactic complexity more commonly studied in birdsong.

The approach taken here, in which call-type sequences are subjected to statistical tests for structural pattern rather than manually inspected, is consistent with a broader recent shift toward data-driven discovery of phonetic and combinatorial structure in animal vocalization. Wang et al. (2024), for example, applied a self-supervised deeplearning model to discover phone-like units and grammar-like sequence patterns in domestic dog vocalizations without relying on hand-specified acoustic categories. The present analysis differs in method — acoustic clustering and permutation-based surrogate testing rather than deep learning — but shares the same underlying goal of letting structure in the data, rather than prior assumptions about what a call type should look like, determine the categories tested.

## Abstract

## 1. Introduction

Since Hauser, Chomsky, and Fitch (2002) proposed that recursion may be the single

computational property that most cleanly distinguishes the human faculty of language in the

narrow sense from communicative capacities shared with other species, comparative research has

largely approached recursion as though it were inseparable from syntax, and by extension from

semantics. That framing produces a difficult testing situation: whenever something recursion-like

is reported in a nonhuman signal, it tends to be received either as evidence of incipient

proto-language or dismissed as an artifact of low-level statistical pattern matching, because the

analytical tools used to look for it are themselves borrowed wholesale from linguistic syntax,

leaving no other outcome available to report.

The empirical picture has moved in interesting directions since then. Fitch and Hauser (2004)

found that cotton-top tamarins could learn finite-state (regular) grammars but failed at

phrase-structure grammars requiring center-embedding, which looked at the time like a genuine

species boundary. Gentner, Fenn, Margoliash, and Nusbaum (2006) complicated the picture by

reporting that European starlings could recognize recursive AnBn patterns under training, and

Corballis (2007) used that result to mount a sustained challenge to the claim that recursion is

unique to human language rather than a more general property of hierarchical cognition. Suzuki,

Wheatcroft, and Griesser (2016) later described compositional syntax in Japanese tit alarm-call

sequences, adding further texture to the sense that structural properties once assumed exclusive

to human language may have partial analogues elsewhere in the animal kingdom.

What is largely missing from this literature is an account of recursion, at the level of the acoustic

signal itself, that does not already presuppose the analytical apparatus of syntax. The existing

evidence base comes from grammar-learning paradigms: trained discrimination tasks that assess

whether an animal can tell an AnBn sequence from an AnBm sequence under laboratory

conditions. These tasks are informative about a cognitive capacity for pattern discrimination, but

they do not tell us whether the vocal signal an organism produces on its own, outside of any

experimental grammar, contains embedded, self-similar structure in the first place. A negative

result in a grammar-learning task does not rule out recursive structure in the naturalistic signal,

and there is currently no standard method for looking for it directly.

## 2. Recursion as a Cross-Disciplinary Construct

Before recursion can be operationalized for bioacoustic analysis, it is worth being explicit about

how differently the term is already used across fields, because each usage carries different, often

unstated assumptions about what recursion requires.

●​ Linguistics (syntax). Recursion is the embedding of a phrase within a phrase of the same

category — a relative clause nested inside a noun phrase, for instance — producing

potentially unbounded hierarchical depth. The formal machinery for this sense of

recursion traces back to Chomsky's (1955/1975) doctoral dissertation, which specified

generative grammars as systems of recursive rewrite rules capable of producing

unbounded structure from a finite rule set; Hauser, Chomsky, and Fitch (2002) later

proposed this same property as the candidate boundary between the human faculty of

language and the communicative capacities of other species.

●​ Music theory (contour). Melodic contours can nest smaller motivic units within larger,

self-similar phrase structures, a formal device studied on its own terms, independent of

any propositional content the melody might or might not carry.

●​ Mathematics (set theory, geometry). Recursion is a function defined in terms of itself,

applied to progressively smaller instances of a problem — the generative logic behind

fractal geometry, where self-similarity holds across scales.

the computational machinery required to parse them. The Chomsky hierarchy

distinguishes regular, context-free, and context-sensitive grammars precisely by the

computational resources — finite-state automaton, push-down automaton, or more —

needed to generate them, which is the formal backbone underlying the tamarin and

describes this kind of cross-field transplantation as "tool migration": the movement of a

propositional meaning, external reference — as though that baggage were part of the construct

## 3. Theoretical Framework: Decoupling Structural Recursion from Semantics

### 3.1 Five embedding topologies

Recursion is not a single structural pattern but a family of related ones, and distinguishing among

them is the first step toward a testable definition. Five topologies, in particular, are worth

separating out before recursion can be tested empirically on an acoustic signal.

●​ Center-embedded (A [B [C] B] A). A unit is nested within a larger unit of the same type,

with material from the outer unit surrounding it symmetrically on both sides at each level

of embedding. Acoustically, this would appear as a contour or motif nested inside a larger

contour, flanked on both sides by material drawn from the same higher-order category.

●​ Tail-end embedded (A [B C] [B C] [B C] …). An initial unit is followed by a fixed

unit-pair that is repeated and appended at the tail, extending the sequence without adding

embedding depth at each step. Acoustically, this looks like an initial element followed by

iterative, self-similar repetition or elaboration at the edge of a call bout, rather than

material surrounding a nested core.

●​ Left-boundary embedded (A [B [C [D]]]). Rather than nesting symmetrically or simply

chaining at the tail, each new unit is embedded one level deeper than the last, with depth

accumulating progressively and asymmetrically rather than being flanked by a matching

outer closure. This produces a cascading, single-sided embedding structure —

schematically a tree that grows deeper at one boundary with each additional unit —

distinct from center-embedding's symmetric bracketing and from tail-end embedding's

flat concatenation.

repeated prefix units front-loaded before that core. The recursion here operates entirely

outside the boundary of the phrase being expanded, rather than modifying its internal

structure.

S) stays fixed, and recursive material is inserted within that fixed frame rather than

prepended outside it. This is structurally the mirror image of external expansion: the

phrase's edges are stable and the recursion happens internally, between them.

left-boundary embedding are the topologies most directly addressed by existing recursive

Two possibilities are worth distinguishing for what, if anything, recursive acoustic structure

apparatus, with no representational function attached. The second is that recursion in acoustics

carries indexical semantics: the recursive pattern reliably indexes an internal or contextual state

compositional combination of meaningful parts. The term itself has roots in Peirce's (1878)

forming part of the linguistic message being conveyed.

mistaking any statistically structured, non-random sequence for evidence of hierarchical

embedding specifically — a signal can differ reliably from a random baseline without containing

Two existing bioacoustic analysis methods map reasonably well onto the operational

within the resulting contour representation, with segmentation and annotation typically carried

Wavelet decomposition represents a signal simultaneously across multiple time-frequency scales,

and Hauser (2004) and Gentner et al. (2006). Those studies asked whether an animal could learn

to discriminate a recursive grammar under operant training — a claim about a cognitive capacity

for grammar learning. The present framework asks a different, and in a sense prior, question:

whether recursive structure exists in the naturally produced signal at all, regardless of whether

the producing organism could pass a grammar-learning task in the laboratory. These questions

are complementary rather than competing, and conflating them is part of why the broader

recursion debate has proven difficult to resolve. A negative result in a grammar-learning

paradigm does not rule out recursive structure in the naturalistic signal, and a positive finding of

recursive acoustic structure does not, on its own, establish a grammar-learning capacity.

### 7.2 Limitations

The framework is agnostic about production mechanism. As formulated here, it cannot

distinguish recursion that arises from centrally organized motor hierarchies from recursion that

arises as an incidental byproduct of peripheral — aerodynamic or biomechanical — constraints

on the vocal apparatus. Resolving that distinction would require pairing the acoustic analysis

proposed here with independent kinematic or neurophysiological data, which falls outside the

scope of a purely acoustic, structural framework and is left for future work.

There is also a more general risk, inherent to any similarity-based method, of finding "recursion"

wherever self-similarity happens to exist for non-recursive reasons — simple repetition without

genuine embedding, or convergent acoustic constraints that produce similar-sounding units

without any hierarchical relationship between them. This is precisely why the null model

specified in Section 4.4 is treated as a required commitment rather than an optional check:

without it, the framework would be as vulnerable to overinterpretation as the

spectrogram-reading intuitions it is meant to replace.

## 8. Conclusion

Recursion has been difficult to study in nonhuman acoustic signals largely because it has been

treated as inseparable from syntax, and syntax as inseparable from semantics. This paper has

argued for pulling those three apart: defining recursion structurally, as hierarchical embedding of

self-similar units; treating indexical semantics, rather than symbolic reference, as the default

explanation for any correlation between recursive structure and context; and specifying four

operational commitments — a segmentation criterion, a self-similarity metric, an

embedding-topology test, and a null model — needed to make recursion a measurable rather than

an impressionistic property of a signal. Existing contour- and wavelet-based analysis methods,

together with the MOMEL/INSTINT pipeline already under development, provide a practical

route to implementing this framework on real recordings. The resulting predictions are falsifiable

and independent of any particular species, which is the central advantage of starting from

structure rather than from syntax: it gives recursion somewhere to be found, or not found, in the

signal itself.
